flashcards.front: bivariate analysis
flashcards.back: a group of statistical techniques that examines the relationship between two variables

flashcards.front: statistical significance
flashcards.back: Statistical significance determines if research results are likely real or just due to chance. It is measured using p-values, typically with a threshold (alpha) of 0.05. If the p-value is below 0.05, the result is likely not random

flashcards.front: null hypothesis
flashcards.back: the hypothesis that there is no significant difference between specified populations, any observed difference being due to sampling or experimental error.

flashcards.front: p value
flashcards.back: A p-value measures the probability that observed study results occurred by random chance, assuming the null hypothesis (no real effect) is true. It ranges from 0 to 1, with a smaller p-value providing stronger evidence against the null hypothesis.

flashcards.front: Does a low p-value indicate a hypothesis is true?
flashcards.back: On its own, no.

flashcards.front: Does a p value measure the size of an effect or importance of a result?
flashcards.back: No -- statistical significance does not always equal real-world significance.

flashcards.front: How do researchers sometimes denote (write a symbol for) a chi square test?
flashcards.back: x<sup>2</sup>

flashcards.front: chi square test for independence
flashcards.back: statistical test to determine whether there is a significant relationship between two nominal or ordinal values.

flashcards.front: categorical variables
flashcards.back: variables whose values are organized into mutually exclusive groups but whose numerical values cannot be used in mathematical operations. Example: hometowns of survey participants.

flashcards.front: contingency table
flashcards.back: a visual representation of across-tabulation of categorical variables to demonstrate all the possible occurrences of categories

flashcards.front: A chi square test is ONLY for nominal or ordinal values.
flashcards.back: True

flashcards.front: correlation
flashcards.back: a relationship between two variables in which their values change together.

flashcards.front: Correlations are only appropriate for two interval or ratio variables.
flashcards.back: True

flashcards.front: Correlation coefficient
flashcards.back: 1 (Perfect Positive): As one variable increases, the other increases proportionally. -1 (Perfect Negative): As one variable increases, the other decreases proportionally. Zero means no correlation, and small values, like -0.1, mean weak correlation.

flashcards.front: normal distribution
flashcards.back: a theoretical distribution in which values pile up in the center at the mean and fall off into tails at either end. (bell curve)

flashcards.front: You survey a group of youth about their levels of depression, and then compare it to an existing data set. What kind of t-test is this?
flashcards.back: One-sample t-test, because you are comparing your survey against pre-existing data.

flashcards.front: You survey a group of people who don't have pets about their anxiety, and then again after they get pets. What kind of t-test do you have?
flashcards.back: This is a paired samples t-test -- same population, two samples.

flashcards.front: You survey two groups of people -- some who have pets and some who don't, about their anxiety. What kind of t-test might be used?
flashcards.back: Independent samples t-test. Two separate groups of people.

flashcards.front: ANOVA stands for...
flashcards.back: Analysis of Variance

flashcards.front: What does ANOVA and t-tests have in common?
flashcards.back: they both compare group means.

flashcards.front: You are studying the effect of an ACT preparation course on ACT scores for indigenous children. You can gather the scores of the children who took part in the preparation course and the scores of similar indigenous children. Which type of t-test would be appropriate to compare the average ACT scores of these two groups and determine if any difference is statistically significant?
flashcards.back: independent samples t-test

flashcards.front: You are studying the differences in income for LGBTQ+ individuals in your city at age 30 compared to straight, cisgender individuals across the country. You had to conduct a survey to collect income information for LGBTQ+ individuals in your community, but were able to use existing data for the group of straight, cisgender individuals. Which type of t-test would be appropriate to compare the average incomes of these two groups and determine if any difference is statistically significant?
flashcards.back: One-sample t-test

flashcards.front: You are trying to test the effect of peer mentoring on a child's success in managing anger at school. You ask children in your study group to rate their level of anger at lunch before they have started peer mentoring, and then again after they have had a peer mentor eat lunch with them daily for a few weeks. Which type of t-test would be appropriate to compare their scores and determine if any difference is statistically significant?
flashcards.back: Paired samples t-test

flashcards.front: If comparing two groups yields a p value of 0.9, would you say that the groups were different in a statistically significant way?
flashcards.back: No. 0.9 is close to 1 -- and a value of 1 would make them identical. Typically we are looking for p values of .05 or less to say that two groups have a statistically significant difference.

flashcards.front: A .05 threshold for a p value means that 5% of tests will yield p-values smaller than .05.
flashcards.back: True -- and these results may be false positives.

flashcards.front: A paired sample t-test can measurements of the same set of people at two different times.
flashcards.back: Yes

flashcards.front: If you take two groups of people, and give one drug A and the other drug b and then compare them, what kind of t-test is it?
flashcards.back: Independent samples, because they are separate groups with separate drugs

flashcards.front: If I have a group of people and I measure their high school graduation rates, and then compare those rates against previously published data, what kind of t-test do I have?
flashcards.back: It's a one-sample t-test

flashcards.front: A one sample t-test compares a group's mean against a reference value; a paired sample t-test takes a group of people and tests those same people twice, before and after an intervention; and an independent sample t-test tests two independent groups of people.
flashcards.back: True

flashcards.front: statistical significance
flashcards.back: Assuming that the null hypothesis is true and the study is repeated an infinite number times by drawing random samples from the same populations(s), less than 5% of these results will be more extreme than the current result

flashcards.front: magnitude
flashcards.back: The strength of a correlation, determined by the absolute value of a correlation coefficient. Correlation coefficients are measured between -1 and +1. -1 means it goes down when the other variable goes down, +1 means it goes up. 0 means there is no correlation.

flashcards.front: dependent variable
flashcards.back: A variable that is dependent on or caused by another variable, which is not manipulated directly but is measured to determine whether the independent variable has had an effect(Grinnell, 2016)

flashcards.front: independent variable
flashcards.back: a variable that is not dependent on another variable but is believe to cause or determine changes in the independent variable; an antecedent variable that is directly manipulated in order to assess its effect on the dependent variable.

flashcards.front: The number of individuals in a study population is represented by...
flashcards.back: N. (it's capital N and that turns out to be important).

flashcards.front: Correlation is represented by a single lowercase number. What is it?
flashcards.back: r

flashcards.front: hypothesis
flashcards.back: A theory-based prediction of the expected results of a research study.

flashcards.front: Ordinal variable
flashcards.back: variables that can be rank-ordered, like level of education, or tax bracket.

flashcards.front: Nominal variable
flashcards.back: Names or categories that are mutually exclusive. Example: hometowns of study participants.

flashcards.front: variable
flashcards.back: A concept with characteristics that can take on different values. Note: variables must be able to vary. The speed of light isn't a variable -- it's a constant.

flashcards.front: mode
flashcards.back: The most frequent value in a data set. For example, the most common given name among the first names of participants in a study.

flashcards.front: median
flashcards.back: The median is the middle value in an ordered dataset, separating the higher half from the lower half.

flashcards.front: A high standard deviation indicates that data is more spread out.
flashcards.back: true

flashcards.front: A low standard deviation means that data is clustered more tightly around the mean.
flashcards.back: true

flashcards.front: Standard deviation is represented by the greek letter sigma
flashcards.back: true

flashcards.front: 68% of the data falls within one standard deviation of the mean.
flashcards.back: true

flashcards.front: When a researcher 'codes' an interview, what does that mean?
flashcards.back: Qualitative coding involves labeling segments of the data in order to facilitate the process of interpretation. Data can include interviews, surveys, focus groups, and other sources.

flashcards.front: correlation
flashcards.back: A correlation is a relationship between two variables in which their values change together.

flashcards.front: continuous variable
flashcards.back: A continuous variable is a variable that can take on any value within a range. A continuous variable takes on an infinite number of possible values within a given range. [More explanation](https://articles.outlier.org/discrete-vs-continuous-variables)

flashcards.front: validity
flashcards.back: The extent to which the scores from a measure represent the variable they are intended to.

flashcards.front: face validity
flashcards.back: The extent to which a measurement method appears “on its face” to measure the construct of interest

flashcards.front: content validity
flashcards.back: The extent to which a measure “covers” the construct of interest, i.e., it's comprehensiveness to measure the construct.

flashcards.front: criterion validity
flashcards.back: The extent to which people’s scores on a measure are correlated with other variables (known as criteria) that one would expect them to be correlated with.

flashcards.front: *Many studies suggest that there is a relationship between viewing violence on television and violent behavioral patterns. With what statistical test would you test this hypothesis? How would you operationalize the variables needed to test this hypothesis vis-a-vis variable structure, nominal or continuous? What would the results of this test look like if this hypothesis was supported?
flashcards.back: Pearson's correlation, with a continuous variable, such as hours of watching violent television, and a second continuous variable like number of aggressive action.

flashcards.front: *Correlation is a test of causation.
flashcards.back: false

flashcards.front: *The number of individuals in a population is represented by
flashcards.back: N (the capital letter is important)

flashcards.front: *The single letter accompanying the correlation score in a correlation statistic result is the letter...
flashcards.back: r (the lowercase is important)

flashcards.front: *Means, medians and modes are measures of central tendency.
flashcards.back: True

flashcards.front: r is a correlation coefficient - what other name does this have?
flashcards.back: Pearson's correlation coefficient

flashcards.front: What's a way to remember a statistically significant p value?
flashcards.back: We want it to be 'Less than five cents! or <.05

flashcards.front: You're comparing two groups -- one with a result of 20% integration of curriculum lessons and one with a response of 75% integration of curriculum lessons. Would you use a t test or a chi square to determine statistical significance, and why?
flashcards.back: A chi square -- because the variables are reported in percentages and are nominal level data (the 'nominal' buckets of 'integration of curriculum lessons')

flashcards.front: Chi square should or should not be used on continuous values/variables
flashcards.back: Should not. Chi square tests are used on nominal variables -- often expressed by percentages of subjects that fall into a bucket that can be labeled with words.

flashcards.front: Can you use ANOVA to compare two groups?
flashcards.back: You can but you shouldn't, because it can artificially inflate your p value.

flashcards.front: What letter do researchers express ANOVA results in?
flashcards.back: Capital F

flashcards.front: Can you use ANOVA on nominal variables?
flashcards.back: No, ANOVA is used to compare means (and means must be based on continuous variables otherwise we couldn't calculate a mean
